Trying to Conceive

Coeliac disease and fertility: what testing and treatment can tell you

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Coeliac disease can affect health beyond the digestive system, so it sometimes belongs in a fertility or recurrent-miscarriage assessment. The evidence is mixed, and treatment is important without being a promise of pregnancy. Understanding what is known can help you choose the next step with your care team.

Why coeliac disease comes up in fertility care

Difficulty conceiving can have several explanations, and sometimes standard investigations do not identify one. Coeliac disease is one condition worth considering in selected people with unexplained fertility problems or recurrent pregnancy loss. It should not be described as the main explanation for most unexplained infertility.

The relationship has attracted more attention over time, but research does not give a single answer for everyone. Detecting and treating previously unrecognized coeliac disease can improve health and may help reproductive health. Many people with the condition conceive and have healthy pregnancies, and a diagnosis does not mean that infertility is inevitable.

What coeliac disease does to the body

Coeliac disease, also spelled celiac disease, is a chronic immune-mediated condition in which gluten triggers damage in the small intestine. Gluten is found in wheat, barley and rye. Genetic susceptibility contributes, but carrying associated genes alone is not a diagnosis.

Damage to the intestinal lining can interfere with nutrient absorption. Symptoms vary: some people have digestive complaints, while others first present with anaemia, fatigue or a problem outside the gut. The absence of obvious diarrhoea does not rule it out. It is different from a wheat allergy or non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, even when some symptoms overlap.

Infertility studies do not all find the same association

Earlier small studies sometimes reported more coeliac disease among people attending fertility clinics. A 2021 meta-analysis, however, found biopsy-confirmed disease in about 0.7% of women with any infertility and 0.6% of those with unexplained infertility. Its authors did not find a higher prevalence than in the general population.

Other research asks a different question: whether people already diagnosed with coeliac disease later receive more reproductive diagnoses. A 2025 database study found associations with several women’s health disorders, including infertility. An observational association does not prove that gluten caused each problem or that diet will reverse it. Differences in participants, testing, treatment and study design help explain why findings vary.

Periods, puberty and menopause need individual assessment

Delayed first periods, infrequent or absent periods and difficulty conceiving have been reported in people with untreated coeliac disease. These changes can also have other causes. Menstrual irregularity is a reason for assessment, particularly with weight loss, nutritional deficiency or persistent digestive symptoms.

Some older reports suggested earlier menopause. A 2026 systematic review supported associations with later menarche and some menstrual disturbances but did not find a statistically clear earlier menopausal age. Do not assume that coeliac disease has shortened your reproductive life or that an absent period necessarily means menopause. Appropriate investigation is more useful than predicting your future from a group average.

What the evidence says about sperm and sexual function

Small older studies described altered sperm movement and shape, lower sexual activity or other sexual-function difficulties in some men with coeliac disease. One study of 28 men reported improvement in some measures after gluten withdrawal, but not in every semen finding. These results do not establish how often a problem occurs today or prove permanent infertility.

A much larger Swedish study compared 7,121 men with biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease with matched controls and found similar overall fertility, measured through the number of children. Semen quality, sexual function and having children are related but different outcomes. Persistent low desire, erectile difficulties or fertility concerns deserve assessment rather than being attributed automatically to coeliac disease.

Nutrient deficiency is one possible contributor

Poor absorption, inadequate intake and unintended weight loss can affect general health and may contribute to reproductive problems. Iron, folate, vitamin B12 and other deficiencies can be relevant, but no single missing nutrient has been established as the explanation for every fertility difficulty associated with coeliac disease.

The useful response is to assess nutritional status and treat confirmed deficiencies, not buy a large collection of fertility supplements. A dietitian can review food intake and a clinician can select blood tests. Replacing a nutrient is important when needed, but it is not a substitute for investigating ovulation, sperm or other possible fertility factors.

Immune and placental mechanisms remain research questions

Researchers have also examined inflammation and autoimmune activity. It is plausible that these processes contribute alongside nutrition, but saying that the body simply diverts energy away from reproduction is not an established explanation of coeliac-related infertility.

In laboratory experiments, antibodies directed against tissue transglutaminase have bound to placental cells and altered their function, including the ability of cells to invade surrounding tissue during placental development. This is a proposed mechanism, not a test that predicts whether an individual will miscarry. Findings in cells cannot by themselves quantify the benefit of a particular treatment during pregnancy.

Pregnancy outcomes depend on more than the diagnosis

Studies have reported associations between coeliac disease and miscarriage, restricted fetal growth, preterm birth and lower birth weight. A 2023 review of observational studies found that several adverse-outcome associations were concentrated in people whose coeliac disease was undiagnosed. Earlier diagnosis was not associated with those outcomes in its subgroup analysis.

This is reassuring about the value of recognition and appropriate care, but it is not proof that treatment removes every risk. Studies differ in how well they record diet, disease activity and other conditions. Your maternity team can consider your nutritional status, symptoms and pregnancy history rather than treating a research percentage as your personal forecast.

What a gluten-free diet can and cannot do

A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the established treatment for confirmed coeliac disease. It removes the trigger for the immune reaction and allows intestinal healing in most people. Symptom improvement, nutritional recovery and reduced disease activity are meaningful goals whether or not you are planning a pregnancy.

Treatment may improve reproductive outcomes in some circumstances, particularly when disease was previously untreated. It does not guarantee conception or prevent every miscarriage. Continue any indicated fertility or recurrent-pregnancy-loss assessment while coeliac disease is being treated. If you are struggling with the diet, practical dietetic support is more useful than blame.

An often-quoted pregnancy study needs context

A study published in 2000 screened 845 pregnant women and identified 12 with coeliac disease. Three already knew their diagnosis but were not following a gluten-free diet; nine were newly confirmed. Seven of the 12 had an unfavourable pregnancy outcome. The report also described six healthy babies born after the women had followed a gluten-free diet for a year.

Those small numbers helped raise an important clinical question. They were not a randomized comparison proving that the diet caused every later healthy birth, and they cannot establish a fixed one-year waiting period or a guaranteed success rate. Larger subsequent studies and current clinical guidance should carry more weight than this single historical report.

Ask about testing before removing gluten

If coeliac disease has not been diagnosed, talk to a clinician before starting a gluten-free diet. Reducing gluten can make antibody tests and intestinal tests less informative. Initial testing commonly involves tissue-transglutaminase IgA antibodies together with total IgA; results and individual circumstances determine the next steps.

A specialist may recommend small-intestinal biopsies or other investigations to confirm the diagnosis. NICE recommends considering testing for unexplained subfertility or recurrent miscarriage, particularly in the wider context of symptoms, deficiencies or family history. This is a targeted clinical decision, not a recommendation that every person with a fertility concern diagnose themselves through a commercial food-sensitivity panel.

If you already avoid gluten or are pregnant

Tell the clinician how long you have avoided gluten and whether coeliac disease was ever formally confirmed. A specialist may discuss records, selected genetic testing or a supervised gluten challenge when appropriate. A positive susceptibility gene alone does not establish coeliac disease, and a challenge is not a routine test to undertake on your own.

Challenge schedules differ; a universal six-to-eight-week home plan is not appropriate. The Celiac Disease Foundation advises against undertaking a gluten challenge while pregnant. If you have confirmed coeliac disease, continue your gluten-free diet during pregnancy. If diagnosis is uncertain and you are already pregnant, obtain specialist advice about a safe diagnostic plan rather than restarting gluten yourself.

Gluten sensitivity and wheat allergy are not equivalent

Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity can involve symptoms such as bloating or discomfort without the characteristic autoimmune intestinal injury of coeliac disease. Wheat allergy involves a different immune response. Evidence about coeliac disease and reproduction cannot simply be transferred to either of these conditions.

There is no established evidence that removing gluten improves fertility in everyone with unexplained infertility or suspected gluten sensitivity. If foods seem to trigger symptoms, seek an assessment that considers coeliac disease before restriction and other possible causes. A dietitian can help make any necessary exclusion nutritionally balanced instead of progressively removing more foods without a clear diagnosis.

Prepare for pregnancy with a nutrition and follow-up plan

If you have confirmed coeliac disease, a preconception appointment can review disease control, persistent symptoms, weight change and nutritional blood results. During pregnancy, a dietitian can help you obtain adequate energy, protein, fibre and micronutrients while staying gluten-free. Check food labels and discuss cross-contact in shared preparation areas.

Folate, iron, vitamin B12, calcium and vitamin D may need particular attention according to your intake and test results. Ask which prenatal supplement and folic-acid dose are appropriate; requirements and local recommendations can differ when absorption is impaired. Do not start high doses independently. Persistent symptoms despite the diet deserve follow-up rather than an assumption that you are simply not trying hard enough.

Do not overlook other reasons for fertility problems

Age-related changes, ovulation disorders such as PCOS, primary ovarian insufficiency, endometriosis, tubal problems, thyroid disease and sperm factors can coexist with coeliac disease. Thyroid disease is especially relevant because autoimmune conditions can occur together. Treating the gut condition does not automatically address these other factors.

A fertility review may consider both partners when applicable. The investigation should follow the history, examination and previous results, rather than repeatedly testing only for coeliac disease. Pregnancy loss also has many possible explanations. Neither a loss nor a delay in conceiving proves that you ate the wrong food or failed to follow a diet perfectly.

When to arrange specialist support

Common fertility guidance recommends assessment after 12 months of trying when the person providing the eggs is under 35, or after six months from age 35. Over 40, earlier assessment is often appropriate. Do not wait for those intervals if periods are absent or very irregular, there is a known fertility risk or you have recurrent pregnancy loss.

Discuss coeliac symptoms or a close family history promptly as part of that review. Planning pregnancy while investigations continue is an individual decision: there is no blanket instruction that everyone who suspects coeliac disease must stop trying until a diagnosis is final. Your gastroenterology, fertility and maternity teams can help balance symptoms, nutrition, age and your preferences.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NICE advises considering coeliac testing in unexplained subfertility or recurrent miscarriage; NIDDK explains diagnosis and established dietary treatment.

Population studies and systematic reviews give mixed reproductive findings. Laboratory mechanisms and small historical studies are kept separate from clinical proof.

How BeMama can help

Bring your symptom history, previous tests, dietary changes and pregnancy goals to the appointment. Fertility difficulties and pregnancy loss are not evidence of personal failure.

When to seek help

Do not remove gluten before diagnostic advice or restart it for a home challenge if already avoiding it. Never undertake a gluten challenge while pregnant; confirmed coeliac disease requires ongoing gluten-free care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Coeliac disease is worth considering in selected fertility assessments, but is not the explanation for every problem.
  • Menstrual, sperm and pregnancy findings differ across studies.
  • A gluten-free diet treats confirmed coeliac disease; it cannot guarantee conception or prevent all losses.
  • Testing should be planned before dietary restriction, with specialist advice if already gluten-free or pregnant.
  • Nutrition support and ordinary fertility investigation can proceed together.

Frequently asked questions

Does coeliac disease always cause infertility?

No. Many people with coeliac disease conceive and have healthy pregnancies. Research findings vary, and the diagnosis alone cannot predict your fertility.

Is it the main cause of unexplained infertility?

That is not established. Some studies find an association, while a 2021 meta-analysis found a low prevalence of biopsy-confirmed disease in infertile women. Testing is considered in context.

Should I try a gluten-free diet before getting tested?

Speak to a clinician first. Removing gluten can affect diagnostic results, making it harder to determine whether coeliac disease is present.

Can a gluten-free diet guarantee a pregnancy or prevent miscarriage?

No. It is essential treatment for confirmed coeliac disease and may help health and reproductive outcomes, but other fertility and pregnancy-loss factors still need attention.

Can men with coeliac disease have children?

Yes. Older small studies described semen or sexual-function changes, but a large population study found similar overall fertility in men with diagnosed disease. Individual concerns still warrant assessment.

Does coeliac disease mean I will have early menopause?

No. Older reports and newer findings are not fully consistent. A recent meta-analysis did not show a clear earlier menopausal age; symptoms require individual evaluation.

Can I do a gluten challenge during pregnancy?

Do not start one. The Celiac Disease Foundation advises against challenges during pregnancy. Ask a gastroenterologist how to investigate safely if diagnosis is uncertain.

Is gluten sensitivity the same condition?

No. It does not have the same characteristic autoimmune small-intestinal injury. Coeliac fertility findings should not be assumed to apply to gluten sensitivity or wheat allergy.

Should everyone take extra folic acid or iron?

The appropriate supplement and dose depend on pregnancy planning, local guidance, diet, absorption and test results. Ask your clinician rather than adding high doses yourself.

Must I wait a year before asking about fertility?

Not always. Assessment is generally earlier from age 35, over 40, with absent or irregular periods, known risk factors or recurrent pregnancy loss. Coeliac symptoms and family history also merit discussion.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
